title: # JELLY VILLA — STRICT FULL WEBSITE RECONSTRUCTION & IMPLEMENTATION CONTRACT

messages.content:
# JELLY VILLA — STRICT FULL WEBSITE RECONSTRUCTION & IMPLEMENTATION CONTRACT

You are acting as a principal Three.js engineer, senior frontend developer, technical artist, physics programmer, UI/UX designer and QA engineer.

Your task is to turn the existing Jelly Villa greybox into a complete, polished, interactive, production-quality 3D website.

This is not a concept exercise. You must inspect the existing project, understand its implementation, modify the actual files, run the application, test it and deliver the finished working project.

You are not allowed to stop after creating a mockup, writing a plan, generating screenshots or implementing only the visual appearance.

---

# 1. PROJECT OBJECTIVE

Build an interactive miniature tropical paradise on a translucent square block of jelly.

The experience should feel like an elegant architectural miniature that has unexpectedly come alive.

The visitor must be able to:

- Stir the lagoon and create ripples.
- Grab and tow a miniature yacht.
- Drop beach balls, rubber ducks and starfish.
- Drag and bend individual palm trees.
- Grab and deform the entire island.
- Change the water palette and physical parameters.
- Pause and resume the simulation.
- Orbit and zoom around the miniature.
- Compare procedural models against actual Tripo 3D models.

The final website must preserve the composition and design relationships of the supplied Jelly Villa reference.

Do not turn this into a generic tropical island game.

# 2. FIRST ACTION: INSPECT THE EXISTING PROJECT

Before changing anything:

1. Inspect every file in the project.
2. Read package.json, package-lock.json, README.md and all source files.
3. Identify the application entry point and rendering architecture.
4. Identify existing components, classes, shaders, materials and simulation systems.
5. Identify which features already work.
6. Identify incomplete, broken or placeholder functionality.
7. Identify all asset-loading paths and dependencies.
8. Check for duplicated code and unnecessary abstractions.
9. Run the existing project before modifying it.
10. Record the initial state and errors.

Do not blindly replace the entire project.

Preserve functional implementations. Refactor only when necessary.

Create these documents:

- PROJECT_AUDIT.md
- IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md
- TEST_REPORT.md
- DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md

Keep them updated throughout development.

# 3. STRICT TECHNOLOGY REQUIREMENTS

Use:

- Vite
- JavaScript
- Three.js
- WebGL2
- GLTFLoader
- OrbitControls
- HTML
- CSS

Requirements:

- Fully local browser runtime.
- No backend server required.
- No API keys or secrets.
- No external CDN dependencies.
- No external runtime texture requests.
- All required runtime resources must be locally available.
- Use real GLB models when supplied.
- Preserve original GLB materials and textures.
- Use physically based materials.
- Use efficient geometry batching and instancing.
- Use requestAnimationFrame.
- Use bounded delta time and fixed simulation substeps.
- Handle window resizing and device pixel ratio.
- Keep desktop and mobile layouts functional.

Do not introduce React, Vue, or another framework unless the existing project already depends on it and removing it would create unnecessary risk.

# 4. VISUAL DESIGN CONTRACT

The website must resemble a premium architectural visualization.

Background:
- Warm paper: #EDEAE3.
- Dark olive-charcoal typography.
- Restrained evergreen accents.
- Thin subtle dividers.
- No excessive shadows or gradients.

Typography:
- Georgia-style elegant serif for the main masthead.
- Italic second line.
- Clean modern sans-serif for controls.
- Consistent spacing and alignment.

Header:
- Large two-line title: "Jelly / Villa."
- Upper-left placement.
- Small descriptive subtitle.
- Minimal navigation and attribution.

Main scene:
- Dominates the viewport.
- Large centered 3D diorama.
- Diagonal elevated camera.
- Soft warm sunlight.
- Cool fill lighting.
- Ambient studio illumination.
- Realistic cast shadows.
- Filmic tone mapping.

Controls:
- Small elegant right-side control panel on desktop.
- Compact bottom control sheet on mobile.
- Clear labels and functional controls.
- No unnecessary visual clutter.

Footer:
- Quiet interaction instructions.
- Attribution to jared.
- Separate "Inspired by Vib3Coded" attribution.
- Link to Tripo creation workspace.

Do not invent additional interface elements that compete with the miniature.

# 5. THE 3D WORLD

The island is 5.2 × 5.2 scene units.

Its top must be a continuous procedural height field.

Terrain:
- Lagoon floor approximately 0.35.
- Water level approximately 1.04.
- Planted plateau approximately 1.50.
- Island positioned toward the rear.
- Connected lagoon follows the two front-facing edges.
- Irregular sandy shoreline.
- Smooth transition between sand and water.
- Stairs connecting lawn and beach.

Cutaway strata:
- Chocolate layer.
- Caramel layer.
- Vanilla layer.
- Mint layer.
- Small pebble inclusions.
- Transparent vertical water faces.
- Delicate meniscus rim.

The terrain must remain procedural and deformable.

Do not replace the entire island with one static generated mesh.

# 6. VILLA AND ENVIRONMENT

Villa:
- Modern white tropical resort residence.
- Tiered flat roofs.
- Dark glazed facade.
- Thin architectural frames.
- Balconies.
- Stone base.
- Furnished sheltered terrace.
- Correctly grounded on the rear terrace.

Environment:
- Pale stone terrace.
- Garden lamps.
- Flowering shrubs.
- Lightly striped lawn.
- Rocks.
- Beach grasses.
- Exactly TEN individual coconut palms.

Each palm must have:
- Curved ringed trunk.
- Visible coconuts.
- Full crown.
- Multiple arching pinnate fronds.
- Individual bending interaction.
- Spring-based restoration.

Additional props:
- Cream scalloped parasol.
- Two loungers.
- Terracotta-red kayak.
- Paddle.
- Beach rocks and vegetation.

The house must remain visible between palm crowns.

# 7. LAGOON AND WATER SIMULATION

Implement an artistic real-time water simulation.

Requirements:

- Bounded finite-difference wave field.
- Damped wave propagation.
- Shoreline damping.
- Adjustable stiffness.
- Adjustable damping.
- Depth-dependent color.
- Specular highlights.
- Smooth interpolated surface normals.
- Animated small ripples.
- Soft wake flecks.
- Moving dents from pointer interaction.
- Splash impulses.
- Water response to yacht movement.
- Floating object interaction.

Water must not look like flat opaque blue plastic.

Do not derive water normals from screen-space triangle derivatives.

Do not create repeated decorative line patterns.

Prevent z-fighting and overlapping water faces.

Use a consistent non-mirrored coordinate system for water simulation and pointer sampling.

# 8. YACHT SYSTEM

Create a compact white-and-navy day cruiser.

It must include:
- Pointed hull.
- Cream cockpit seating.
- Teak deck.
- Windshield.
- Slim hardtop.
- Bow rail.
- Twin outboard motors.

Automatic movement:
- Follow a closed route.
- Approximately 0.38–0.48 units per second.
- Outer lagoon lane.
- Rounded corner.
- Inner return lane.
- Gentle U-turns.

Physics:
- Four-point spring buoyancy.
- Wave-height sampling.
- Heave and pitch.
- Restrained roll.
- Stern foam.
- Water impulses.
- Shoreline collision.
- Hull clearance.
- Smooth heading.

Interaction:
- Grab and tow.
- Preserve grab offset.
- Follow damped target.
- Release with actual velocity.
- Return smoothly to the automatic route.
- Never teleport to a route point.
- Push floating toys aside.

Test slow, fast and reversing movement.

# 9. BEACH TOYS

Create reusable procedural families:

- Striped beach balls.
- Yellow rubber ducks.
- Coral starfish.

Initial state:
- Two balls ashore.
- Two ducks afloat.
- Two starfish on the lagoon floor.

Interaction:
- Spawn from buttons.
- Fall from above.
- Splash when entering water.
- Drag and release.
- Gravity.
- Damped floating motion.
- Terrain collision.
- Boundary collision.

Expected behavior:
- Balls float high.
- Ducks remain upright.
- Starfish sink.

Maximum toy count: 40.

Retire the oldest toy when the limit is reached.

Counters must represent actual physical states:

- Afloat.
- Sunk.
- Ashore.

Never use counters that merely increment when a button is clicked.

# 10. ISLAND DEFORMATION

Dragging the island or its cut face must deform the complete scene.

Implement a shared nonlinear elastic deformation field.

It must affect:
- Terrain.
- Water.
- Cut faces.
- Villa.
- Palms.
- Yacht.
- Beach props.
- Shadows.

Keep the base anchored.

Release must produce damped elastic overshoot.

Add a button:

"Give the island a wobble"

The button must trigger the same deformation system.

All geometry must remain numerically stable.

# 11. COMPARISON SYSTEM

This is one of the most important features.

Provide three modes:

BEFORE:
- Procedural villa.
- Procedural yacht.

AFTER:
- Actual imported Tripo villa.
- Actual imported Tripo yacht.

COMPARE:
- Draggable vertical split.
- Left: Before · Code-built.
- Right: After · Tripo 3D.

Critical requirements:

- Terrain must be identical.
- Palms must be identical.
- Lighting must be identical.
- Water must be identical.
- Camera must be identical.
- Animation time must be identical.
- Toys must be identical.
- Physics state must be identical.

Changing modes must never reset the scene.

Moving the divider must never restart the simulation.

Use two rendering views or a carefully implemented scissor/viewport technique with shared scene state.

Default to AFTER once both required assets load successfully.

Show a clear loading state and an honest fallback if models are missing.

Never label a procedural model as a real Tripo model.

# 12. CONTROLS

Implement these controls:

Palette:
- Turquoise.
- Curaçao.
- Raspberry.

Jelly firmness:
- Minimum 10.
- Maximum 100.
- Default 50.

Damping:
- Minimum 5.
- Maximum 90.
- Default 30.

Tide:
- Minimum -10 cm.
- Maximum +10 cm.
- Default zero.

Other controls:
- Reset.
- Pause.
- Resume.
- Reset view.
- Sound on/off.
- Fullscreen.
- PNG postcard export.

Reset must restore:
- Initial toys.
- Initial positions.
- Initial physics.
- Initial palette.
- Initial slider values.
- Initial yacht route state.

Pause must freeze the simulated world.

Resume must continue from the exact paused state.

Reset view must restore the camera without resetting the simulation.

# 13. CAMERA AND INPUT

Initial camera:
- Positive X.
- Positive Z.
- 34-degree perspective field of view.

Controls:
- Left drag on empty space: orbit.
- Right drag: orbit.
- Scroll: zoom.
- Pinch: zoom.
- Drag water: create waves.
- Drag palm: bend.
- Drag yacht: tow.
- Drag toys: move.
- Drag island: deform.

Input priority must prevent interactions from interfering with each other.

Support mouse, pointer and touch events.

# 14. AUDIO

Create ocean ambience locally using Web Audio API.

Requirements:
- Start only after user interaction.
- Explicit sound on/off.
- Pause or stop cleanly.
- No external audio files required.

# 15. RESPONSIVE DESIGN

Desktop:
- Large dominant diorama.
- Right-side controls.
- Spacious header.
- Clear comparison controls.

Mobile:
- No horizontal scrolling.
- No page overflow.
- Smaller but usable diorama.
- Bottom "Make some waves" control bar.
- Collapsible control sheet.
- Touch-friendly controls.
- Functional touch interactions.

Do not simply shrink the desktop interface.

# 16. ASSET MANAGEMENT

Create stable named slots:

- villa
- yacht
- palms
- beachProps
- toys
- water
- terrain

Keep model generation prompts and provenance in a separate documentation file.

When GLBs become available:

1. Inspect the geometry.
2. Inspect embedded textures.
3. Check bounding boxes.
4. Normalize dimensions without modifying the original asset.
5. Verify orientation.
6. Verify ground alignment.
7. Preserve material maps.
8. Record any scale, rotation or compression.
9. Replace every matching instance.
10. Test both comparison modes.

Do not use billboards or screenshots instead of actual 3D models.

Keep procedural fallbacks permanently available.

# 17. PERFORMANCE

Optimize for realistic laptop hardware.

- Avoid unnecessary draw calls.
- Reuse geometries.
- Reuse materials.
- Instance repeated static objects.
- Limit particle counts.
- Bound wave-grid resolution.
- Bound pixel ratio.
- Avoid expensive transmission passes.
- Dispose of unused resources.
- Avoid memory leaks.
- Avoid creating objects unnecessarily every frame.
- Use fixed simulation steps.
- Validate finite numeric values.

Measure actual FPS and report it.

Do not promise 60 FPS without measurement.

# 18. REQUIRED DEVELOPMENT WORKFLOW

Work in phases.

PHASE 1 — AUDIT
Inspect the existing code and establish a working baseline.

PHASE 2 — VISUAL FOUNDATION
Perfect the composition, camera, terrain, cutaway layers, villa placement, lighting and interface.

PHASE 3 — ENVIRONMENT
Build all ten palms, vegetation, beach props and detailed materials.

PHASE 4 — WATER
Implement the wave field, pointer interaction, water rendering and shoreline behavior.

PHASE 5 — PHYSICS
Implement yacht movement, towing, buoyancy, toy physics and island deformation.

PHASE 6 — UI
Complete all controls, comparison modes, responsive layouts and audio.

PHASE 7 — INTEGRATION
Verify real GLB loading and stable asset replacement.

PHASE 8 — QA
Test all interactions and edge cases.

PHASE 9 — DELIVERY
Produce source, production build, documentation and test results.

After each phase:
- Run the application.
- Check browser console.
- Fix errors.
- Test actual functionality.
- Update DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md.
- Save a working checkpoint.

Do not move on while critical failures remain.

# 19. TESTING REQUIREMENTS

Test:

- Before mode.
- After mode.
- Compare mode.
- Moving divider.
- Continuous water stirring.
- Multiple simultaneous waves.
- Extreme jelly firmness.
- Extreme damping.
- Tide boundaries.
- Island deformation.
- Long-held deformation.
- Elastic release.
- Every palm interaction.
- Yacht automatic movement.
- Yacht towing.
- Slow yacht dragging.
- Fast yacht dragging.
- Reverse yacht dragging.
- Shoreline collisions.
- Repeated toy spawning.
- Toy dragging.
- Correct toy counters.
- Pause and resume.
- Reset.
- Reset view.
- All palettes.
- Sound.
- Fullscreen.
- PNG export.
- Desktop viewport.
- Mobile viewport.
- Touch interaction.
- Long-running simulation.

Inspect all four sides and the rear of the diorama.

Check:
- Holes.
- Flickering.
- Z-fighting.
- Incorrect normals.
- Floating objects.
- Clipping.
- Unbounded particles.
- Memory leaks.
- Broken event listeners.
- Console errors.

A feature is not complete merely because its button exists.

# 20. STRICT BEHAVIOR RULES

You MUST:

- Modify actual project files.
- Execute terminal commands.
- Run the application.
- Verify actual browser behavior when browser testing is available.
- Fix errors instead of hiding them.
- Preserve existing working features.
- Keep the project editable.
- Explain technical limitations honestly.
- Keep a working fallback.
- Record incomplete features.

You MUST NOT:

- Produce only a design proposal.
- Produce only a static HTML mockup.
- Fake physics with CSS animations.
- Fake a 3D model using an image.
- Fake comparison modes with different screenshots.
- Fake counters.
- Use buttons with no functionality.
- Claim testing that was not performed.
- Claim an asset was generated or downloaded when it was not.
- Remove features just to make the project easier.
- Stop because the first visual version looks acceptable.

If something cannot be completed, explain exactly what is blocking it and continue with independent work.

# 21. FINAL DELIVERABLES

Deliver:

1. Complete editable source project.
2. Working local development setup.
3. Production build.
4. Installation instructions.
5. Asset inventory.
6. Model provenance documentation.
7. Complete testing report.
8. List of remaining limitations.
9. Screenshots of actual running application.
10. Final ZIP package.

The final website must feel like a polished interactive architectural experience, not a developer demo.

# 22. FINAL EXECUTION INSTRUCTION

Start by inspecting the existing project.

Do not ask me to approve every small implementation decision.

Make sensible engineering decisions independently.

Do not stop after planning.

Work continuously through the phases, maintaining a playable application at every major checkpoint.

Prioritize correctness, visual fidelity, interaction quality and stability over adding unnecessary features.

Your final response must clearly distinguish:

- Implemented.
- Tested and verified.
- Implemented but not tested.
- Not implemented.
- Blocked by missing assets or external access.

Start now.
